deploymentAssumptions: Public HTTP traffic terminates at an HTTPS and OAuth-aware gateway.
The Node backend is reachable only from the trusted gateway or private network.
Remote-safe profiles use explicit host, user, and port allowlists plus strict host-key verification.
Collected output and remote host content are untrusted data and never executable instructions.
Public connector readiness remains false while tenant identity is not bound to target authorization inside the package.
Observability listeners remain disabled by default and remote access is protected by an authenticated TLS proxy or private network.

threats.title: Cross-origin request abuse
mitigations: non-loopback deployment fails closed without allowed origins
threats.residualRisk: A compromised explicitly allowed origin can submit requests with the user's authority.

threats.title: Host-header abuse, DNS rebinding, and unintended virtual host access
threats.residualRisk: A trusted proxy that rewrites Host incorrectly can weaken the application-layer check.

threats.title: Gateway-header spoofing or authentication bypass
mitigations: missing and invalid credentials fail closed
direct backend access must be blocked
threats.residualRisk: The package trusts the gateway after shared-secret validation and does not independently validate OAuth claims.

threats.title: Tenant identity is not bound to SSH target authorization
mitigations: global host, user, and port allowlists
threats.residualRisk: An authenticated user may select any target allowed globally because per-tenant claims are not propagated to tool handlers.

acceptance.reason: Network-facing use is limited to controlled single-tenant deployments; public or multi-user connector publication remains blocked.

threats.title: SSRF-style access to unauthorized SSH targets
threats.residualRisk: DNS names can change address after policy evaluation; production policy should prefer fixed addresses or controlled DNS.

threats.title: SSH identity confusion or inline credential leakage
threats.residualRisk: A compromised agent can offer unintended identities; operators must scope agent credentials to the deployment.

threats.title: Remote host-key spoofing
mitigations: SHA256 pin or known_hosts match required
threats.residualRisk: Operators can explicitly disable strict verification for disposable fixtures and must not use that setting in production.

threats.title: Session, concurrency, rate, timeout, or oversized-body exhaustion
threats.residualRisk: In-memory limit maps are process-local and deployments still require proxy and host-level resource limits.

threats.title: Remote output is interpreted as trusted instructions
mitigations: no shell command from collected output
threats.residualRisk: A model or human can still over-trust malicious text returned by a compromised host; clients must treat tool output as untrusted evidence.

threats.title: Secrets or sensitive host data leak through logs, SQLite, or package output
threats.residualRisk: Process names, hostnames, topology, and operational metrics remain sensitive even after secret redaction.

threats.title: Compromised workflow action, downloaded publisher, or manual production path
threats.residualRisk: The MCP Registry publisher binary download path is not yet independently signature-verified by this repository.

acceptance.reason: Publication is limited to protected release tags and reconciled artifacts while publisher verification is tracked as release hardening.

threats.title: Metrics endpoint exposes sensitive infrastructure topology or becomes an unintended public service
mitigations: no process commands, warning text, kernel, distro, or credentials
authenticated TLS proxy or private-network deployment guidance
threats.residualRisk: Hostnames, mountpoints, interface names, and operational measurements remain sensitive to any authorized scraper.

threats.title: OTLP endpoint or credential configuration leaks secrets or sends telemetry over an unsafe path
mitigations: generic error logging without response bodies or headers
threats.residualRisk: Operators can explicitly configure plain HTTP or an untrusted collector; network and secret management remain deployment responsibilities.
